Portal site

This bundle is also a private site inside the GreenGuard portal at portal.greenguard-usa.com/gtm. Sign in by magic link with your GreenGuard email; access is granted by role, so ask Dan if the link does not let you in.

The site carries the plan, timeline, training, targets, outreach, discovery, objections, competitive, reports and the partner and site pages, plus a Claude assistant for the program. Target scores and Dan's approve column sync with the Google Sheet, and call reports write to HubSpot.

Refresh it after editing this bundle:

node app/scripts/build-gtm-content.js    # rebuild the site content from these files
bash app/scripts/gtm-docs-refresh.sh     # refresh the assistant's copy of the docs

Three rules that override everything else

  1. Dan approves every target row before the first touch. Claude researches and drafts; the MBA sends; Dan can take sending back at any time.
  2. Prices come from mqtt.greenguard-usa.com/sparkbridge/pricing only. Partner terms come from /sparkbridge/partners only. No per-tag numbers, no discounts beyond the program, no roadmap promises.

Sources of truth when this bundle and something else disagree

Live site > this bundle. SparkBridge repo docs/gtm/ > this bundle's copies. Google Sheet approve column > CSV approve column.

Files marked INTERNAL

Not for prospects. The design partner offer is an unpublished end-customer offer; the product themes document is internal strategy.

01-plan/mba-90-day-gtm-sprint.html:
SparkBridge 90-Day Go-to-Market Sprint

MBA Program Owner Playbook, adjusted 2026-09-07

Objective: validate SparkBridge's market position with real Ignition integrators, convert qualified firms into Architecture Partners, and create the pipeline for the first production deployments.

Primary owner: MBA / Go-to-Market Program Lead. Duration: 90 days. Start: the day the MBA has the access checklist in section 25.

Changes from the 2026-09-07 draft

The draft was written without sight of what already exists. These are the adjustments; everything not listed stands as written.

  1. Target list exists. 31 firms, contacts re-verified 2026-09-07, 2 to 3 named people per firm, email pattern per firm. Days 6 to 14 become "score and extend", not "build". Outreach can begin day 8.
  2. Partner program terms are ratified and live. Section 16 quotes them exactly. The MBA may quote those terms and nothing else.
  3. Sending. Assumption: the MBA sends outreach from their own greenguard-usa.com mailbox and LinkedIn, only to rows Dan has approved in the target sheet. Dan can revert to sending himself; the rest of the plan does not change.
  4. Success metrics. The "target" tier is the KPI set Dan accepted from the final pre-launch review. Minimum and exceptional tiers rescaled around it.
  5. Verticals. Four priority verticals, chosen from where the target list has depth. Others opportunistic. Re-rank at day 30 on replies.
  6. Training exists with a certification. Section 5 uses it instead of an ad hoc test.
  7. Honest-limits rules added (section 6). They are what makes the answer believed.
  8. Prices added (section 17). The live pricing page is the only source of truth.
  9. CRM conventions added (section 13). HubSpot properties and pipeline are fixed.
  10. Architecture review ownership named: Dan plus Claude. Pre-read before, written review within two business days after.
  11. Product calendar added (section 24). 3.0.0 lands mid-October inside the sprint.
  12. Touch 3 assets named. Nothing else is sent.
  13. Leadership review at day 30, 60 and 90 with Dan; Claude compiles the numbers.
  14. Access checklist added (section 25).
  15. The seven discovery questions from the SE training are the required opening set on every call.

1. Mission

The MBA's job is not primarily to sell software licenses in 90 days.

The job is to run a disciplined market-validation and partner-acquisition sprint answering:

  1. Which integrators have the distributed-estate problem SparkBridge solves?
  2. Which verticals have the strongest pain?
  3. Which messages generate technical interest?
  4. What objections repeatedly appear?
  5. Where does SparkBridge fit into real architectures?
  6. Which integrators can become long-term channel partners?
  7. Can we create 1 to 2 serious production deployment opportunities?

Target outcome:

30 approved targets
        v
8 to 12 replies
        v
5 to 8 technical conversations
        v
3 to 5 architecture reviews
        v
2 to 3 Architecture Partners
        v
1 to 2 production pilots
        v
Production proof

2. Role definition

Title: SparkBridge Go-to-Market and Partner Development Lead.

This is not a cold-calling sales role. It combines market research, partner development, customer discovery, technical sales coordination, messaging validation, competitive intelligence, CRM discipline and go-to-market experimentation.

3. Core principle

Do not sell a module. Sell the conversation:

What changes when your Ignition deployment reaches 40 sites?

Core messaging, in the words the site uses:

  • The problem: scaling Ignition creates backend complexity.
  • The architecture: Edge moves data. Provider carries it. Host turns it into one system.
  • The operating principle: publish once. Add consumers when you need them.
  • The differentiation: MQTT is the transport. Operating the estate is the problem.
  • The adoption story: nothing gets torn out on day one. Keep the plant. Replace the fragile connections between plants.

Never lead with "we have a cheaper MQTT module". That makes SparkBridge a commodity. Lead with architecture.

4. What success looks like at day 90

Metric Minimum Target (accepted KPIs) Exceptional
Approved targets researched and scored 30 30 50
Personalized first touches sent 20 30 45
Replies 5 8 to 12 16+
Technical conversations 4 5 to 8 12+
Architecture reviews delivered 2 3 to 5 7+
Architecture Partners signed 1 2 to 3 4 to 5
Production pilots started 0 1 to 2 2, one in measured production
Objection database, vertical ranking, repeatable process yes yes plus one written measured deployment

5. Week one: product immersion

Days 1 to 2: SparkBridge SE training

Use 02-training/SparkBridge-SE-Training-v1.pdf (16 modules) with the price cheat sheet open throughout. Order and timings are in the training README inside the PDF. Modules 00a and 00b cover Ignition itself; do not skip them.

Certification, as defined by the training: quiz passed at 80% or better (SparkBridge-SE-quiz.pdf), the demo script run once for Dan or an engineer, one discovery call shadowed.

Oral check before any outreach:

"An integrator has 35 remote Ignition sites, one central application, and wants to add a historian. Explain how SparkBridge changes the architecture."

The answer must contain: sites publish once over Sparkplug to a broker; Host builds one namespace; the historian is a consumer at Host (SparkVault) so nothing changes at the 35 sites; store-and-forward covers the WAN gaps on source timestamps; site 36 is one more Edge.

Also be able to explain SparkBridge in 30 seconds, 2 minutes and 10 minutes.

Day 3: website and sales asset immersion

Read in this order, all in 12-site-pages/ as PDFs and live on mqtt.greenguard-usa.com/sparkbridge: Overview (live), Compare, Architecture (Choose Your Starting Point table), Pricing, Partners (04-partner-program/), Roadmap, Benchmarks. Then the 40-site reference architecture PDF (03-reference-architecture/).

Required assignment, one page: what problem SparkBridge solves; who has it; what it replaces; what it does not replace; why an integrator would care; why they might not; when SparkBridge should not be recommended. Knowing when not to sell is the point.

Day 4: competitive training

Training module 08 and 10-competitive-cheat-sheet.md. The category distinction to hold:

MQTT modules  ->  connect Ignition to MQTT
SparkBridge   ->  architecture for operating distributed Ignition estates

Keep the cheat sheet as a living document. Every conversation adds a row or corrects one.

Day 5: messaging certification

Be able to answer, unprompted:

  • "What is SparkBridge?" A distributed data architecture for Ignition that separates plant data production from the applications and systems that consume it.
  • "Isn't this just MQTT?" MQTT is the transport, and the right one. SparkBridge is what remains after the transport: one namespace, consumers that scale on the shared stream, replay on source timestamps into history and warehouse, enrollment, fleet, policy.
  • "Why not existing MQTT modules?" If the requirement is connecting Ignition to MQTT, they are a good answer and we say so. SparkBridge matters when many sites, independent consumers, fleet operations and governance have to grow without revisiting plants.
  • "Do I have to replace my Ignition system?" No. Nothing gets torn out on day one.

6. Honest limits the MBA carries into every conversation

These are the caveats the site publishes. Say them before the prospect finds them.

  • No published production reference yet. Every number was measured on named hardware with reproduction steps in the reference architecture. The partner program exists to produce the first case study.
  • Never say "certified". The Sparkplug Compatible listing is in progress; we ran the TCK harness.
  • Early access and pilot labels: SparkRecord (early access 0.1.0), SparkValidate (pilot), GitOps / Enterprise Governance (pilot). Buy the labeled products for what they do today.
  • Enrollment in 2.9.0 issues certificates but the broker does not yet require the client certificate at connect. Say "certificate issuance", never "mTLS enforced". 3.0.0 closes this.
  • Mixed-vendor Edge and Host pairing is by specification; we run the exact pairing on the bench before anyone buys.
  • Modules are signed with our own code-signing certificate, not an Inductive Automation one; the gateway asks to trust it once.
  • Team size: say it honestly if asked. Development is free with no time limit, so a prospect can prove everything on their own estate before spending.

Pattern: answer, then the caveat, then stop.

7. Days 6 to 14: score and extend the target list

The list exists: 06-targets/integrator-targets.csv, 31 firms, refreshed 2026-09-07 with 2 to 3 named people per firm, email pattern and confidence per firm, and Dan's approve column. Google Sheet "SparkBridge Partner Targets" in Drive mirrors it.

Days 6 to 10: score all 31 with the rubric in section 8 (columns score_*, score, tier are in the CSV, blank). Verify any row marked unverified or pattern before it goes out. Rows Dan has not approved are not contacted.

Days 11 to 14: extend to 50 using the same columns. Look for: significant Ignition practice, multi-site customer deployments, distributed SCADA, MQTT or Sparkplug experience, enterprise industrial customers, custom application work, long managed-support relationships. The research notes in 06-targets/integrator-targets-research-notes.md show the evidence standard.

Priority verticals, from where the list has depth and where the design partner offer already points:

  1. Distributed manufacturing (DMC, Flexware, Corso, ATS, RoviSys, Tamaki)
  2. Water, wastewater, utilities and renewables (SAGE, Perceptive, Brown, NeoMatrix, Ulteig, Vertech)
  3. Data centers (Hanley, Thermo, BW Design Group, NFM, BIJC, Vertech)
  4. Oil and gas (Streamline, CSE ICON, NFM)

Opportunistic: pharma and validated (SL Controls/NNIT, Agidens, 4IR), food and beverage, mining, logistics (no logistics-specific Ignition integrators surfaced in search).

8. Score every target

Criteria Score
Large Ignition practice 0 to 5
Multi-site deployments 0 to 5
MQTT / Sparkplug experience 0 to 5
Target vertical fit 0 to 5
Enterprise customer evidence 0 to 5
Likely distributed architecture pain 0 to 5
Public technical sophistication 0 to 5

Maximum 35. Tier A 25 to 35: direct personalized outreach. Tier B 18 to 24: secondary outreach. Tier C under 18: monitor.

Most important question per firm: what evidence suggests this company has a distributed systems problem? Do not contact someone merely because they use Ignition.

9. Days 8 to 30: outreach sprint

Philosophy: no brochures, no feature dumps, no long introductions, no immediate demo ask. Lead with an architectural question. The objective is curiosity and a technical conversation.

Primary message (full text and follow-up in 07-outreach/):

What changes when your Ignition deployment reaches 40 sites?

We built SparkBridge around that question. Sites publish once, so applications, historians, warehouses and other consumers can be added centrally without revisiting every plant.

We are looking for a small group of experienced Ignition integrators to pressure-test the architecture against real distributed estates. If you have a topology worth discussing, we would like to compare approaches.

Rules: one named person per firm at a time, the firm-specific hook from the CSV in sentence one, plain text, no tracking pixels, UTM only on the two links. Dan approves the row before the first touch. Every send logged in HubSpot the same day.

10. Outreach sequence

Touch When Content
1 Architecture question Day 0 Short personalized email or LinkedIn message. Goal: a reply.
2 Specific observation Day 3 to 5 Reference their distributed project, industry, MQTT experience or multi-site work.
3 One technical asset Day 8 to 10 Exactly one: Compare page, 40-site reference architecture PDF, Benchmarks page, or one finished article from 14-articles/. Not everything.
4 Partner program Only after relevance is established "We are forming a small group of Architecture Partners and thought your team may be a strong fit." Link to /sparkbridge/partners.

A "no thanks" closes the deal as lost and cancels the remaining touches. Silence after touch 4 goes to a 60-day hold.

11. The first discovery call

Integrator speaks 70%, SparkBridge 30%. Discovery, not demonstration.

Required opening set (SE training module 07), every call, answers into HubSpot before the call ends:

  1. How many Ignition gateways, and which are redundant pairs? (shape)
  2. How do sites reach the center today: Gateway Network, MQTT, VPN, nothing? (shape)
  3. What is the busiest central box doing right now, CPU and memory? (the pain number)
  4. What happens to history and alarms when a site's WAN drops?
  5. How many consumers of site data exist, and who is asking for the next one?
  6. Who builds a new site gateway and how long does it take?
  7. Is there a broker already, and who owns it?

Then, as time allows: growth (at what site count does architecture become difficult; have customers added historians or warehouses later; have you revisited sites to add a consumer; what becomes painful after 20 sites), competitive (what MQTT stack, why, what you wish it did differently), validation (does SparkBridge solve a problem you actually meet; where does it not fit; what would stop you recommending it). Full script in 08-discovery-call-and-report.md.

Hand off to the architecture review for any estate over ten sites, any HA question, any broker the customer already runs, any 8.3-only feature.

12. Every conversation produces a structured report

Within 24 hours, in HubSpot on the contact and deal (template and field mapping in 08-discovery-call-and-report.md): account, architecture (site count, current shape, MQTT stack, central applications, existing consumers), pain (primary, secondary, business consequence, current workaround), SparkBridge fit (strong / moderate / weak / unknown), objections in the prospect's exact words, next step.

The intelligence database is worth more than the lead count.

13. CRM conventions (fixed)

  • HubSpot contact properties: outreach_campaign = sparkbridge-fap-2026-09, outreach_segment = vertical, lifecycle lead.
  • One contact per named person, one company per firm.
  • Deals: the "SparkBridge Partners" pipeline (create once in the HubSpot UI; the MCP integration cannot create pipelines) with stages contacted, call booked, review delivered, partner signed, pilot live, production measured. Until it exists, deals go in the default Sales Pipeline tagged "SparkBridge FAP". Deal created at first reply.
  • Every deal carries: named owner, next action, next meeting date, architecture status, technical blocker, commercial blocker, target deployment date. No deal sits labeled "interested".

14. Architecture review program

This is the primary conversion mechanism. Offer: draw your estate before you buy anything. Intake is the mailto on mqtt.greenguard-usa.com/sparkbridge/architecture-review (site count, topology, tags per site, update rates, WAN type, history design, applications, pain points, Ignition versions).

SparkBridge delivers: current-state diagram, SparkBridge reference architecture, failure-domain analysis, migration path, rough sizing with the list price for that shape, known limitations and open questions.

Ownership:

  • MBA: scheduling, intake, documentation, follow-up, CRM, opportunity progression.
  • Dan plus Claude: Claude prepares a one-page pre-read from the intake (architecture number from the Architecture page, list price for the shape, honest limits, partner terms) at least one day before the call; Dan leads the technical conversation; Claude drafts the written review within two business days; Dan approves it before it goes out.

The written review is the deliverable that qualifies a firm as an Architecture Partner.

15. Days 31 to 60: convert conversations into reviews

By day 30 know: which verticals respond, which messages work, which objections repeat, which firms have genuine fit. Double down on evidence. If manufacturing produced five conversations and data centers none, move the effort. This is a market-discovery sprint, not a fixed campaign.

Build the objection library (09-objection-library.md): product, commercial, market, trust. Track objection, frequency, severity, response, product action. Review weekly with Dan.

16. Days 45 to 75: Architecture Partner conversion

Terms (ratified 2026-09-05, live at /sparkbridge/partners). Quote these and nothing else:

  • Architecture Partner: invitation only, cap 10. Entry condition: one completed architecture review of an estate of 10 or more sites. Benefits: development licenses (free for everyone, stated so partners know), NFR production-grade key per module for the partner's demo estate renewed yearly, direct engineering access, 90-day deal registration, 20% off list, named escalation with a one-business-day reply on production issues, co-selling on request, one recorded training session per year, quarterly roadmap call.
  • Founding Partner: the first five Architecture Partners to take a customer estate into measured production. 40% off list on that first production estate, NFR keys that never expire, shared priority support channel, a vote on public roadmap order, joint case study.
  • No discount stacking. Volume pricing is Dan's call, not a discount the MBA offers.
  • Design partners are end customers, not integrators: a separate unpublished 50% offer (05-design-partner-offer-INTERNAL.md) used through the integrator. Never quoted to an integrator as their own discount.

Ideal first partner: a technically strong Ignition integrator with a real distributed customer opportunity and enough engineering depth to challenge SparkBridge. One of those beats ten passive partners.

17. Prices the MBA may quote

Only from mqtt.greenguard-usa.com/sparkbridge/pricing; the cheat sheet PDF is a copy verified 2026-09-06. Per gateway, one-time, development free with no time limit, support optional at 20% of list per year, nothing per tag, device or client.

Shape, 40 sites Required total Support per year
Customer's own broker: 39 Edge + 1 Host $40,300 $8,060
Provider HA pair + history: 39 Edge + 2 Provider + 2 Host + SparkVault $49,780 $9,956
Complete operating architecture: above + FleetOps + Sentinel + GitOps $69,765 $13,953

Site 41 is one more Edge, $995. Never invent a per-tag number; explain the model once and show the 40-site example.

18. Production opportunity qualification

Score: real customer, multi-site, active project, architecture pain, executive support, technical fit, timeline under 12 months, each 0 to 5. Prioritize 25 or more.

19. Days 61 to 90: pipeline conversion

Conversation -> Architecture review -> Technical validation -> Partner discussion -> Customer opportunity -> Pilot / deployment

For each pilot agree the measurement plan up front (sites, tags per site, outage replay, consumer count) so the first write-up can use the same method as the Benchmarks page.

20. Weekly operating rhythm

  • Monday: pipeline review (new targets, outreach, responses, meetings, reviews, opportunities) and product intelligence review (objections, competitive findings, feature requests, website confusion).
  • Tuesday to Thursday: research, outreach, discovery calls, follow-up, review coordination.
  • Friday: one-page weekly report to Dan (11-reports/weekly-report-template.md).

21. Leadership review at day 30, 60 and 90

Present evidence, not activity. Claude compiles the numbers from HubSpot beforehand.

Bad: "I sent 80 emails." Good: "Eight integrators responded. Six immediately understood the 40-site problem. Three use remote tag providers. The repeated objection is new-vendor risk, not pricing."

Dan asks: what did we learn, what changed, what should we stop, what should we double down on, is this a product issue or a messaging issue.

22. KPI dashboard

Leading: target quality, personalized outreach, response rate, discovery calls, architecture reviews. Validation: problem acknowledged, fit, partner interest, technical follow-up requested. Commercial: qualified opportunity, pilot, deal registration, partner agreement. Strategic: most promising vertical, most common architecture, most common objection, most common competitor, feature gaps. Template in 11-reports/.

23. What the MBA should not do

  • Become a generic SDR: mass automated email, LinkedIn spam, feature dumps, "just checking in", volume as the metric.
  • Become product support: document questions, coordinate escalation.
  • Promise roadmap items. Never "we can add that". Instead: "I will document that requirement and have the product team evaluate where it fits." Any "when does X ship" goes to the public roadmap page, which has no dates on purpose.
  • Discount. New-vendor risk is answered with architecture access, engineering support, NFR licensing, pilot support and transparent evidence, not price.

24. Product calendar during the sprint

  • Today: SparkBridge 2.9.0 released 2026-09-06 (both Ignition lines). SparkRecord 0.1.0 early access. SparkS7 0.2.1.
  • Mid-October (target week of 2026-10-12): SparkBridge 3.0.0, a breaking release that partners will prove: manual-ack transport, client-certificate enforcement, two-round enrollment. Partners starting in the sprint install 3.0.0, not 2.9.0.
  • After: SparkRecord 0.2.0, SparkInject 0.2.0, SparkNotify 0.3.0.
  • Externally: no dates. Internally: do not sell 2.9.0 enrollment claims that 3.0.0 corrects (section 6).

25. Access checklist (before day 1)

  • greenguard-usa.com mailbox and calendar; a booking link for review calls.
  • HubSpot seat with edit rights; the "SparkBridge Partners" pipeline created.
  • Edit access to the Google Sheet "SparkBridge Partner Targets" and the Drive folder Claude uploads / Industrial & Drivers.
  • LinkedIn from a personal account with the company listed.
  • This bundle, and the SparkBridge repo docs/gtm/ if the MBA will edit the source files.
  • A standing 30-minute Monday slot with Dan and the Friday report address.

26. Required deliverables at day 90

  1. Market validation report: who has the problem, which verticals care, at what scale pain appears, the strongest buying trigger.
  2. Target market ranking: vertical, integrator type, customer architecture, deployment size.
  3. Objection report: frequency, severity, recommended response, product implications.
  4. Competitive intelligence report: Cirrus Link, Gateway Network, HiveMQ, EMQX, Cedalo, custom architectures, as heard in the field.
  5. Partner pipeline: active, qualified, in review, production opportunity, closed / no fit.
  6. Product feedback report: critical gap, strategic opportunity, nice-to-have, off-architecture distraction (apply the four themes in 13-product-themes-INTERNAL.md).
  7. Recommended GTM strategy, from evidence, not assumptions.

27. Timeline

Days Phase Output
1 to 7 Learn: training, certification, competitive, messaging Can explain and position SparkBridge independently
6 to 14 Map: score 31, extend to 50, tier Ranked, approved target list
8 to 45 Discover: personalized outreach, conversations Validated pain points, repeatable messaging
31 to 60 Validate: architecture reviews, technical validation Real-world architecture fit
45 to 75 Partner: partner discussions, production opportunities 2 to 3 serious partner relationships
61 to 90 Convert: alignment, pilot 1 to 2 credible production opportunities

Final instruction

Your job is not to prove SparkBridge is amazing. Your job is to discover where SparkBridge is genuinely valuable. Be curious. Ask technical questions. Listen more than you pitch. Document objections exactly. Look for patterns. Do not defend the product when someone says it does not fit; that answer is valuable.

After 90 days, success means the company knows who to sell to, what problem to lead with, what objections to solve, which partners matter, and where the first production deployments will come from.

04-partner-program/partner-program-terms.html:
SparkBridge Architecture Partner program (ratified terms)

Status: RATIFIED by Dan 2026-09-05 and published at mqtt.greenguard-usa.com/sparkbridge/partners (expanded page live 2026-09-06). This file is the internal record of the terms; the live page is what a partner sees. Invitation only. Ten Architecture Partner seats, five Founding.

Goal

Ten integrators who consider SparkBridge part of their standard architecture toolkit for distributed Ignition estates.

Architecture Partner

Who: an integrator with an Ignition practice that has deployed, or is scoping, an estate of 10 or more sites and has completed one SparkBridge architecture review with us.

Benefit Terms
Development licenses Unlimited, every module, no time limit (already true for everyone; stated so partners know it)
NFR licenses One production-grade key per module for the partner's own demo estate, renewed yearly at no charge
Architecture support Direct access to the engineers who built the modules, by email and scheduled call, for any estate the partner is designing
Deal registration Registered opportunities are protected for 90 days; we do not quote the end customer directly on a registered deal
Partner discount 20% off list on every license the partner resells or deploys
Engineering escalation Named contact, reply within one business day on production issues
Co-selling We join technical calls with the partner's customer on request
Training One remote architecture and deployment session per year, recorded for the partner's team
Roadmap access Quarterly roadmap call; partner requests logged and answered

Founding Partner

The first five Architecture Partners to take a customer estate into production on SparkBridge.

Benefit Terms
Permanent internal development entitlement The NFR keys above never expire and survive any later change to the partner program
Priority support channel Shared channel with our engineers; production issues first in the queue
Discounted first production deployment 40% off list on the first production estate
Roadmap participation Founding partners vote on the order of the roadmap items on the public roadmap page
Joint case study We write it, they approve it, both names on it, or anonymized at their request

What we ask of partners

  • One completed architecture review before the first production quote.
  • Production issues reported with the gateway diagnostics bundle.
  • Permission to list the partner by name on the partners page (optional, per partner).

Decisions (Dan, 2026-09-05)

  1. Partner discount 20% off list. No stacking with volume pricing or any other discount.
  2. Founding discount 40% off list on the first production estate, every module in that estate.
  3. NFR scope: one production-grade key per module for the partner's own demo estate.
  4. Deal registration window 90 days.
  5. Invitation only; the page is public so an invited firm can read the terms.
  6. Design partners (end customers, 50%) stay a separate unpublished offer: design-partner-offer.md.

Title: A North American {vertical} operator running {N} Ignition gateways

  1. Previous architecture. Hub gateway, backends, remote tag providers, where history was written. One diagram.
  2. Problem. The box that was overloaded, the outage that lost data, the consumer that could not be added. Numbers: CPU, memory, tag count, sites, outage duration.
  3. Deployment. Edge count, Provider shape, Host shape, consumers added, in what order, over what period. What was not migrated and why.
  4. Measurements. Before and after: hub load, replay after a real outage, consumer add time, time to provision a new site. Every figure tied to the machine it came from.
  5. Results. What the operations team says now. What they would do differently.

Rule: no figure appears in a case study that the design partner has not seen and approved in writing. Nothing is published before a production deployment exists.

Subject

What changes when an Ignition deployment reaches 40 sites?

Body

Hello {first name},

GreenGuard USA has been building and benchmarking an alternative architecture for distributed Ignition deployments that have outgrown backend fan-in, remote tag provider scaling and per-site history pipelines.

SparkBridge separates the estate into three roles. Edge publishes once at each site and buffers to disk through an outage. Provider carries the data under per-site identities and deny-by-default permissions. Host turns many sites into one namespace and fans it out to consumers on MQTT 5 shared subscriptions, so adding a historian or a warehouse changes nothing at the sites.

We documented a 40-site reference architecture covering WAN outages, timestamp preservation, consumer scale-out and standby recovery, with every figure tied to the machine it was measured on: https://mqtt.greenguard-usa.com/sparkbridge/compare https://mqtt.greenguard-usa.com/sparkbridge/benchmarks

Would a 30-minute call with one of your Ignition architects make sense in the next two weeks?

{Dan's signature} GreenGuard USA

08-discovery-call-and-report.title: Discovery call script and call report
08-discovery-call-and-report.html:
Discovery call script and call report

Before the call

Read the CSV row and the HubSpot record. Know the firm's published multi-site project. Have the Architecture page's Choose Your Starting Point table and the cheat sheet open. Set the frame in the first minute: "This is a discovery call, not a demo. I want to understand how you build distributed estates today."

Integrator speaks 70%, you 30%.

The seven questions, every call (answers into HubSpot before the call ends)

  1. How many Ignition gateways, and which are redundant pairs? (shape)
  2. How do sites reach the center today: Gateway Network, MQTT, VPN, nothing? (shape)
  3. What is the busiest central box doing right now, CPU and memory? (the pain number)
  4. What happens to history and alarms when a site's WAN drops?
  5. How many consumers of site data exist, and who is asking for the next one?
  6. Who builds a new site gateway and how long does it take?
  7. Is there a broker already, and who owns it?

One vertical question

Vertical Ask
Multi-site manufacturing Which plant is the hub, and what breaks when it goes down?
Water, wastewater, utilities What links reach the lift stations, and what does a month of data cost?
Oil and gas Who audits your EFM and batch records, and how do you prove a row never changed?
Data centers, facilities Is the UPS and the chiller in the same screen as the process?
Pharma, food, validated How many weeks does the validation package take, and who types it?
Integrator (always) How many estates over ten sites are you scoping this year?

As time allows

Growth: at what site count does the architecture get hard; have customers added a historian or warehouse later; have you revisited sites to add a consumer; what becomes painful after 20 sites. Competitive: what MQTT stack do you use, why, what do you wish it did differently. Validation: does SparkBridge solve a problem you actually meet; where does it not fit; what would stop you recommending it.

Closing the call

Any estate over ten sites, any HA question, any broker they already run, any 8.3-only feature: offer the free architecture review and name the intake link. Otherwise agree one concrete next step with a date. Never end on "interested".

09-objection-library.title: Objection library
09-objection-library.html:
Objection library

Seeded 2026-09-07 from SE training module 11. Add every new objection in the prospect's exact words. Review weekly with Dan. Pattern for every answer: answer, then the caveat, then stop.

Categories: Product (missing feature, integration, performance, security), Commercial (pricing, licensing, support, procurement), Market (no demand, existing solution sufficient, estate too small), Trust (new vendor, no references, longevity).

# Category Objection (exact words) Frequency Severity Response Caveat we say out loud Product action
1 Commercial "What happens to the price when we add tags?" Nothing. Per gateway, per product. Tags, devices and clients are never counted; the 40-site examples do not move when the estate gets busier. Edge has a 250,000-tag budget per gateway; past that you add a gateway, not a fee. none
2 Market "We already run Cirrus." Keep the transport. What we add sits after the broker: shared-subscription consumers, history and warehouse on source timestamps, enrollment, fleet view, generated policy. Start with Host on your broker. Mixed-vendor edge and host pairing is by specification; we run your exact pairing on the bench before you buy. interop bench record per pairing
3 Commercial "Why pay for Provider when we have HiveMQ / Mosquitto?" You do not have to. Edge and Host connect through any conformant broker; Provider is for the customer with no broker or who wants generated per-site policy without ACL files and with no client count. HiveMQ and Mosquitto 2.1 are the brokers that have run on our bench. none
4 Commercial "What happens if support lapses?" The software keeps running exactly as before. You stop receiving new versions and support until you renew. None. none
5 Trust "Early access and pilot: is this production software?" Edge, Host, Provider, Vault, Inject, Passage, FleetOps, Sentinel, Flow and the drivers are released and live-proven on both Ignition lines. SparkRecord 0.1.0 is early access, SparkValidate and GitOps are pilots, labeled that way on every page. Buy the labeled ones for the problem they solve today, not for the roadmap. none
6 Trust "Do you have a reference customer?" Not a published one yet. Every number we print was measured on named hardware with reproduction steps. The partner program exists to produce the first case study; Founding Partners get a joint one. Never name a customer or imply one. If a reference is a precondition, say so to Dan and route to the design partner conversation. first measured deployment
7 Product "8.1 or 8.3?" Both. Every product ships signed on both lines and is proven on a live 8.3 gateway before release. Same price. The 8.3 line is newer; ask engineering about any 8.3-only feature before promising it. none
8 Trust "Are you Sparkplug certified?" We have run the Eclipse TCK harness and the Sparkplug Compatible listing is in progress. We do not use the word certified until it is granted. That is the caveat. listing request
9 Trust "The gateway warned me about the module certificate." Modules are signed with the SparkBridge code-signing certificate, not one issued by Inductive Automation, so the gateway asks to trust it once. Every release bundle includes the signature and the live proof record. An IA-issued certificate is on the list; no date. IA signing
10 Market "Isn't this just MQTT with a markup?" MQTT is the transport and the right one. What you pay for is what remains after it: one namespace built from births, consumers that scale on the shared stream, replay on source timestamps, enrollment, fleet, policy. The compare page lists it row by row and says where the standard alone gets you the same cell. At five sites, use what Ignition gives you; we say that on the compare page. none
11 Commercial "We want a subscription / monthly price." We sell one-time licenses with optional 20% support. There is no monthly option. Volume pricing by site count is Dan's call, not a discount the MBA offers. none
12 Trust "Who supports this? You are a small company." Direct engineering support is what the 20% buys: the people who wrote the modules. Every module has a manual, a live proof record and a review record in its release bundle. Development is free so you can prove it on your own estate before you spend. Say the team size honestly; do not inflate it. none
13 Product "Can Passage / IEC-104 / DNP3 write to equipment?" No. Passage is read only; the utility drivers read only. Edge write-back is off by default and allowed only for listed devices and points. BACnet and Logix drivers do write; say which is which. none

13-product-themes-INTERNAL.title: SparkBridge product themes (internal)
13-product-themes-INTERNAL.html:
SparkBridge product themes (internal)

Status: internal product-strategy document, 2026-09-05. Not published. The public roadmap (/sparkbridge/roadmap) stays detailed and item-by-item; this file is the filter every new item passes through before it reaches that page.

Why this exists

The public roadmap lists ten capabilities. Each is justified on its own, but a list of ten justified items is not a strategy. Without a frame, the next customer request becomes the next roadmap row and the architectural thesis erodes one reasonable-sounding feature at a time.

The thesis, in one line: publish once at the site, add consumers at the Host, and run the whole estate from one chair. Sites and consumers scale on separate lines. Nothing at a site changes when a consumer is added.

The four themes

Every shipped module, every roadmap row, and every incoming request lands in exactly one theme.

1. Operate

Run a 40 to 200 site estate from one team without visiting sites.

4. Scale

Sparkplug Compatible listing Administrative; Eclipse WG request in Dan queue

Feature-accumulation check (external review 2026-09-06)

The reviewer's five questions, asked before any new product, driver, connector or convenience module:

  1. Does it reinforce Edge -> Provider -> Host?
  2. Does it create a reusable platform capability?
  3. Does it benefit multiple customers?
  4. Does it strengthen one of the four pillars?
  5. Does it reduce operational complexity at scale?

A new driver passes 3 and rarely 1, 2 or 5: drivers stay a separate per-gateway line and never enter the SparkBridge roadmap table. Same for isolated Ignition conveniences (Gantt).

Intake rule for new requests

A request goes on the roadmap only if all four answers are yes:

  1. Which theme? Name one. If it does not fit any, it is a parking-lot item, not a roadmap row.
  2. Does it advance the thesis? It must make publish-once, add-consumers-later, or run-from-one-chair more true. A feature that adds a per-site touch, a per-consumer change at the site, or a new licensing dimension (per tag, per client) is rejected on that ground alone.
  3. Is it measurable? State the number that will be printed on the site when it ships and the bench that will produce it. No number, no row.
  4. Who asked, and how many? One customer request is evidence, not a mandate. Two design or founding partners asking for the same thing inside the same theme is a mandate.

Requests that pass go to the roadmap table with the theme recorded in the commit message. Requests that fail go to docs/internal/PARKING-LOT.md with the theme they almost fit and the reason they failed, so the answer to the customer is written once.

Ownership

Someone has to hold this frame against the queue. Until a product owner exists, Dan is the product owner and this file is the checklist; Claude applies it when drafting roadmap rows and flags any row that fails a question rather than adding it. The Solution Architect role (the one that draws estates with partners) feeds requests in; it does not decide what ships.

Sequencing, unchanged

The release ordering in ~/.claude/plans/what-remains-for-sparkbridge-tranquil-blossom.md stands: 2.9.0 additive (Operate: enrollment + capacity), SparkRecord 0.2.0 (Move Data), 3.0.0 breaking batch (Trust: trace wire hops; Move Data: manual-ack transport; hardening), with the partner proof track in parallel feeding site should-adds 4 through 9.
